headline: New Zealand's election ends with no clear winner

sources.title: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election (BBC News)
New Zealand faces weeks of uncertainty with election 'too close to call' (The Guardian)
'Too close to call': Wait begins for special votes after cliffhanger Election night (RNZ)

chunks.text: New Zealand, a country in the South Pacific, held an election on November 7, 2026. In [[preliminary results]], Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's center-right National Party won the most seats in parliament, 42. The main [[opposition party]], center-left and led by Chris Hipkins, won 36. Each got about 29 percent of the [[party vote]], which decides each party's seats. Hipkins has not {{given up}}. He said it may take longer to {{figure out}} what voters wanted.

verbs.correct: To stop trying and accept a loss
verbs.wrong: To give a speech to supporters
verbs.why: Our team never gives up, even when we are far behind. She gives up when a puzzle gets too hard. Hipkins has not given up, although his party has fewer seats.

verbs.wrong: To count all the votes again
verbs.why: I can never figure out the bus schedule. My son figures out new phones faster than I do. Hipkins said it may take longer to figure out what voters wanted.

chunks.text: Most governments in New Zealand are [[coalitions]], groups of parties that agree to rule together. Luxon's government has National and two smaller [[right-leaning]] parties. Support for both partners {{went up}} from the 2023 election. The three parties' seats {{add up to}} 67. Extra seats under the voting rules give parliament 131 members on the early count. A [[majority]], more than half, is 66. That [[slim lead]] means the government could {{hold on to}} power.

verbs.why: Rent goes up almost every year in big cities. The price of coffee goes up when there is a bad harvest. Support for the government's two smaller partners went up.
Small savings add up to a lot of money over time. Two short walks a day add up to an hour. Together, the three parties' seats add up to 67.

verbs.correct: To keep something you already have
verbs.wrong: To share power with a rival
verbs.why: Good companies hold on to their best workers. Many families hold on to old photos for years. With a slim lead, the government could hold on to power.

chunks.text: Opportunity, a small [[centrist]] party, {{won over}} about 6 percent of voters and will enter parliament for the first time. Even with Opportunity's 7 seats, Hipkins and his partners {{fall short of}} a majority. Opportunity's leader said it would {{reach out to}} the party with the most seats first. But hundreds of thousands of [[special votes]], from people overseas or away from home, still need counting. An [[election law]] expert said the result could {{come down to}} small [[margins]].

verbs.wrong: To ask people to vote early
verbs.why: A friendly waiter wins over even the hardest customers. A good first speech wins over many new voters. The small centrist party won over about 6 percent of voters.

verbs.correct: To fail to reach a goal
verbs.wrong: To lose a seat in a close race
verbs.why: Our fundraiser often falls short of its goal. His test score falls short of what the college wants. Even with Opportunity's 7 seats, Hipkins and his partners fall short of a majority.

verbs.correct: To contact someone to start talking
verbs.wrong: To make a promise to voters
verbs.why: Good teachers reach out to parents when a child has trouble. Our company reaches out to new customers by email. Opportunity's leader said it would reach out to the party with the most seats first.

verbs.correct: To be decided mainly by something
verbs.wrong: To be counted again by hand
verbs.why: Many close games come down to the last few minutes. A job choice often comes down to pay. An election law expert said the result could come down to small margins.

chunks.text: The [[official result]] {{comes out}} on November 27. Until then, Luxon will {{stay on}} as prime minister of a [[caretaker government]], a temporary government that keeps [[daily business]] going. Talks between parties could {{drag on}} for weeks. The campaign focused on the [[cost of living]] and [[unemployment]]. [[Record numbers]] of New Zealanders have {{moved away}}, many to Australia. Together, the two biggest parties won under 60 percent, their lowest [[share]] since 1996.

verbs.why: The new school rules come out every August. Test scores come out a week after the exam. The official election result comes out on November 27.

verbs.correct: To keep the same job for longer
verbs.why: Some teachers stay on for a year after their planned last day. The old manager stays on until the new one arrives. Luxon will stay on as prime minister until the official result.

verbs.correct: To last longer than people want
verbs.wrong: To be kept secret from voters
verbs.why: Some meetings drag on for hours. The winter drags on when it is cold and dark. Talks between the parties could drag on for weeks.

verbs.correct: To leave and live somewhere else
verbs.wrong: To lose a job in a slow economy
verbs.why: Many young people move away from small towns for work. Some retired couples move away to be near their grandchildren. Record numbers of New Zealanders have moved away, many to Australia.

wordDefs.def: Early numbers that may still change before the final count
ex: The preliminary results of the medical test look good.
Preliminary results show that the new drug may help.
The company shared preliminary results from its survey.

wordDefs.def: A party that is not part of the government
ex: The opposition party voted against the new tax.
Leaders of the opposition party asked the prime minister hard questions.
Each opposition party hopes to win the next election.

wordDefs.def: A vote for a political party, not for one person
ex: In some countries, voters cast a party vote and a vote for a person.
The party vote decides how many seats each party gets.
She gave her party vote to a small new party.

wordDefs.def: Groups of parties or people that agree to work together
ex: Small countries often form coalitions to have a stronger voice.
Several coalitions of parents asked for safer streets.
Coalitions can fail when partners disagree.

wordDefs.def: Having political views closer to the right side
ex: My uncle reads a right-leaning newspaper.
The city has many right-leaning voters.
A right-leaning group wants lower taxes.

wordDefs.def: More than half of a group or total
ex: A majority of students voted for a longer lunch break.
The plan needs a majority to pass.
The majority of my friends live near the city.

wordDefs.def: A very small advantage over others
ex: Our team has a slim lead with five minutes left.
The mayor holds a slim lead in the latest poll.
A slim lead can disappear very quickly.

wordDefs.def: Having political views in the middle, not left or right
ex: The centrist candidate tried to please both sides.
Many centrist voters care most about the economy.
A centrist group of lawmakers wrote the new plan.

wordDefs.def: Votes cast by people away from home or overseas, counted later
ex: Special votes can take weeks to count.
Students studying abroad can send special votes.
In a close race, special votes can change the winner.

wordDefs.def: The rules about how elections are run
ex: She teaches election law at a university.
The new election law changes when people can register to vote.
Lawyers who know election law are busy in a close race.

wordDefs.def: The differences in votes or points between winners and losers
ex: Both games were won by small margins.
The margins in this year's races were very close.
Polls show wide margins in some cities.

wordDefs.def: The final count that is approved and announced
ex: We are still waiting for the official result of the vote.
The official result showed a different winner from the early count.
The official result will be posted online.

wordDefs.def: A temporary government that runs things until a new one starts
ex: A caretaker government usually avoids big new laws.
The country had a caretaker government for three months.
Ministers in a caretaker government still do their daily work.

wordDefs.def: The normal work that must be done every day
ex: The manager is away, but the daily business of the store continues.
Phone calls and emails are part of my daily business.
The strike stopped the daily business of the city hall.

wordDefs.def: The amount of money people need for food, housing and other basics
ex: The cost of living is very high in New York.
Many workers want higher pay because of the cost of living.
She moved to a smaller town with a lower cost of living.

wordDefs.def: The state of not having a job, or the number of people without jobs
ex: Unemployment is lower this year than last year.
The factory closing caused high unemployment in the town.
He received help during his time of unemployment.
Record numbers of people visited the park in July.
Record numbers of students joined the class.
Stores saw record numbers of shoppers on Black Friday.

wordDefs.def: The part of a total that belongs to one person or group
ex: Her share of the rent is 600 dollars.
Online sales are a growing share of the market.
Each child got an equal share of the cake.

mainIdea.s: New Zealand's two biggest parties finished almost even, so nobody has clearly won yet. Small parties and votes from overseas will help decide which side forms the next government.
mainIdea.why: The vote was too close for any party to give up or claim a win. The final count comes out on November 27, and talks could drag on for weeks.

mainIdea.s: The prime minister's party lost its place as the largest group in parliament. Now the main opposition will lead the talks with small parties, and a final count is due in late November.
mainIdea.why: Close, but Luxon's National Party still won the most seats. Its government could hold on to power, and Luxon will stay on as prime minister for now.

mainIdea.s: Voters in New Zealand have approved a plan to change how members of parliament are chosen. The new rules start at the next election and will end the separate vote for a political party.
mainIdea.why: This story is about an election with no clear winner. The two big parties are almost tied, and the result could come down to small margins.

tf.s: Neither big party won enough seats to rule without partners.
tf.why: National won 42 seats and the main opposition won 36. A majority is 66, so each party falls short of it alone.

tf.s: Hipkins has given up and accepted that his side lost.
tf.why: Hipkins has not given up. He said it may take longer to figure out what voters wanted.

tf.s: Support for the government's two smaller partners went up.
tf.why: Both right-leaning partner parties got more votes than at the last election.

tf.s: The centrist party Opportunity has been in parliament for many years.
tf.why: Opportunity won over about 6 percent of voters and will enter parliament for the first time.

tf.s: Hundreds of thousands of special votes still need counting.
tf.why: These votes from overseas and away from home are not counted yet, so the result could come down to small margins.

tf.s: Luxon has left his job as prime minister while the votes are counted.
tf.why: Luxon will stay on as prime minister of a caretaker government until the official result.

lines.text: Did you see the election in New Zealand? Nobody won outright.
I saw. It was a real [[photo finish]] between the two big parties.
Both got about 29 percent of the party vote, and Hipkins hasn't {{given up}}.
He said it may take a while to {{figure out}} what voters wanted.
So who forms the next government? For now, [[anything can happen]].
Doesn't Luxon's side have more seats?
Yes. With its two partners, the seats {{add up to}} 67. A majority is 66.
So they could {{hold on to}} power.
Maybe. But hundreds of thousands of special votes still need counting.
They could. One expert said it may {{come down to}} small margins.
What about that centrist party, Opportunity?
It {{won over}} about 6 percent of voters. Its leader plans to {{reach out to}} the party with the most seats first.
So a small party might help [[call the shots]].
It might. The official result {{comes out}} on November 27, and Luxon will {{stay on}} until then.
And after that, the parties have to [[cut a deal]].
Right, and the talks could {{drag on}} for weeks.
With prices so high and so many people {{moving away}}, I hope they move fast.

expressions.def: A race or contest that ends so close that the winner is hard to tell
ex: The 100-meter race was a photo finish.
The vote for class president was a photo finish.

expressions.def: Used to say that the result is not decided and could still change
ex: The game is close, so anything can happen in the last minute.
It is a long race, and anything can happen.

expressions.def: To be the small thing that decides a result
ex: A strong interview can tip the scales in your favor.

expressions.def: To be the person or group that makes the decisions
ex: My older sister calls the shots when our parents are away.
In this office, the manager calls the shots.

expressions.def: To reach an agreement after talks
ex: The two companies cut a deal to share the building.
The city cut a deal with the workers to end the strike.
